item.title: Enhancing Stock Market Forecasting Under Market Turbulence: A Regime-Aware BiMT-TCN with Volatility-Weighted Training and Backtesting
item.description: Forecasting daily stock-index returns becomes especially difficult when volatility changes abruptly. We develop BiMT-TCN, which combines a bidirectional long short-term memory (BiLSTM) network, a modified Transformer (MT) encoder, and a temporal convolutional network (TCN). Within each historical window, these components represent ordered context, interactions between nonadjacent lags, and patterns at several temporal scales. The training loss gives additional weight to high-volatility observations, while a separate, ex-post regime split is used to report normal-and crisis-period errors. Across the experiments on the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE), Hang Seng Index (HSI), and NASDAQ Composite, BiMT-TCN has lower reported errors than the recurrent, convolutional, and Transformer baselines, including on crisis days. Under a simple long-short simulation, its forecasts also produce the highest cumulative returns and Sharpe ratios among the compared rules. The evidence is descriptive rather than a claim of live-trading profitability, but it shows that emphasizing turbulent observations can improve forecast performance in the markets studied.
item.authors: Guangyang Tian;Wuzhida Bao;Xiong Wang;Yao Chen;Yin Yang;Shiping Wen;

item.title: A Survey of Distributed Fiber-Optic Sensing for Wind Turbine Blade Condition Monitoring: From Sensor Deployment to Intelligent Diagnosis
item.description: Reliable condition monitoring of wind turbine blades (WTBs) is essential for operational safety and maintenance cost reduction. Despite the distinct advantages of distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) in providing continuous, full-field monitoring with high spatiotemporal resolution and electromagnetic immunity, a dedicated review synthesizing its application in WTB monitoring is currently lacking. Driven by a systematic bibliometric analysis of the past decade, this comprehensive survey outlines a four-stage technical roadmap of DFOS-based blade monitoring: (i) blade structural modeling and fiber deployment; (ii) optical signal processing and feature extraction; (iii) intelligent fault diagnosis; and (iv) emerging enabling technologies such as digital twin synchronization and shape sensing. Furthermore, this review discusses critical bottlenecks including sensor embedding, spatial resolution and accuracy trade-offs, and long-term durability. By bridging the gap between raw optical sensing and intelligent diagnosis, this survey provides an essential structured reference for both academia and industry.

item.title: Dual-Pool MocoRank: A Controllable Accuracy–Class-Balance Frontier for Student Engagement Detection
item.description: Automated student engagement detection from short webcam clips involves a trade-off between overall accuracy (Acc) and recognition of rare disengagement states. In the Comprehensive Multi-modality Online Student Engagement Dataset (CMOSE), engaged clips comprise about 69% of the data, so Acc can be high even when minority-class recall is low. This study examines two controls over this trade-off: the class composition of the comparison pool during ordinal contrastive training and the post-hoc rule that maps a frozen representation to class labels. Dual-Pool Moco-Rank (DPMR) controls the training-time comparison distribution with balanced and natural-prior stratified pools mixed by $\alpha$. After training, we fit the validation-selected threshold and multinomial logistic regression decision rules using either the scalar score or the score with the 256-dimensional pre-score embedding. Together, these controls produce a selectable accuracy-class-balance frontier on CMOSE. In the closest single-model fixed-threshold comparison, DPMR obtains 76.00% Acc and 57.62% AvgAcc. Its average per-class accuracy (AvgAcc) is 1.88pp above the published MocoRank with Center Loss result and 3.32pp below the published MocoRank-only result of 60.94%. These results support control over the operating point. They do not establish a new single-point record. Code and configuration files are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
item.authors: Mahmoud A. Salem;Islam I. Osman;Mohamed S. Shehata;Abdallah Mohamed;

item.title: Optimal Resilient Bipartite Containment Control for Multi-Agent Systems via Coded Event-Triggered Scheme
item.description: This paper investigates the optimal bipartite containment control problem for multi-agent systems (MASs) under compound false data injection attacks, involving both additive and multiplicative forms. To enhance communication security, a coded event-triggered scheme is designed, only transmitting a w-length string at each trigger event. A neural network (NN)-based reinforcement learning algorithm is proposed under the Identifier-Critic-Actor to solve the challenge of obtaining an analytical solution for the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman partial differential equation. For actor and critic NNs, unlike existing methods that design update rates based on the Bellman residual, we propose a gradient descent algorithm using a simple positive function to simplify the construction of the update law. Lyapunov stability analysis shows that all signals remain bounded, and the followers under both cooperative and antagonistic interactions converge to the respective convex hulls formed by the leaders. Simulation results further verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

item.title: Biomedical Knowledge Graphs and Large Language Models: A Critical Engineering Survey
item.description: Medical language models are fluent but hard to audit. Combined with language models, knowledge graphs offer structured, source-grounded facts. However, recent work often treats a knowledge graph as proof of grounding without verifying whether the system retrieved and used relevant subgraphs or produced clinically safe output. Our survey follows a small set of representative systems through their full lifecycle: graph construction and updating, indexing, retrieval, reasoning, verification, and post-deployment monitoring. We classify integration methods by where and how tightly graphs and models combine, distinguishing simple prompt-pasting from graph-aware encoders, and map the underlying ontologies, clinical datasets, and benchmarks supporting retrieval and tool-using agents. We find that graph benefits are highly conditional. Graphs help when they fill genuine knowledge gaps, entity linking succeeds, retrieval returns small relevant subgraphs, and evaluations use matched text-retrieval baselines. They help less and may hurt when coverage is thin, mappings fail, or retrieved context overpowers decisive evidence. We also examine practical failure modes, including weak citations, poor temporal handling, and closed-loop feedback, in which model proposals are written back into the graph and later retrieved as independent evidence.
item.authors: Rangan Das;Sounak Ghosh;Utsav Bandyopadhyay Maulik;Sushmit Dasgupta;Sanghamitra Bandyopadhyay;Ujjwal Maulik;

item.title: Fuzzing Large Language Model Agents: A Taxonomy, Engineering Framework, and Evaluation Protocol
item.description: Agents powered by large language models (LLMs) increasingly operate as closed-loop decision systems that retrieve external context and memory, plan actions, invoke tools, and alter environment state. This autonomy creates trajectory-level risks, including indirect prompt injection, memory poisoning, unsafe tool invocation, authorization violations, and erroneous environment-conditioned actions, which cannot be assessed adequately by prompt-level testing alone. This paper presents a taxonomy and engineering framework for fuzz-testing LLM-based agents. We formulate agent fuzzing as structured perturbation over user instructions, retrieved context, memory states, tool parameters, and environment feedback, and organize the design space by interaction surface, mutation strategy, execution environment, behavioral safety evaluator, and behavioral coverage objective. The framework integrates seed construction, semantics-aware mutation, trajectory-guided exploration, sandboxed execution, runtime monitoring, behavioral coverage feedback, risk scoring, and failure reproduction. A controlled study with 900 sandboxed trajectories across file-management, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), email, and database scenarios illustrates the workflow. It shows that semantics-aware and state-guided mutation strategies uncover more testbed failures than rule-based mutation. We further discuss evaluator reliability, long-horizon testing, memory safety, multi-agent interactions, scalability, and external validity.
